title: So Much For Your Network
author: Corporate Unspiral
summary: The Corporate Unspiral examines the painful gap between what professional networks appear to offer and what they actually deliver when it matters most. When a career transition arrives, the colleagues who praised your work for years, the leaders who promised introductions, and the peers who offered to put in a good word often go silent—not out of malice but because the shared context of work has dissolved, they are protecting their own standing, or they simply never expected to be taken up on the offer. The article distinguishes four levels of professional relationship that networking culture conflates: recognition (someone knows who you are), rapport (they like talking to you), respect (they think you do good work), and advocacy (they are willing to speak up for you when there is nothing in it for them). Most large networks contain many people at the first three levels and very few at the fourth. The piece argues this doesn't make networking useless—it creates possibilities—but it means you should stop expecting advocacy from every contact. The most important insight is that when silence arrives, it rarely reflects your value: the constraints of the other person are almost always the better explanation.
points: A network produces four distinct types of relationship: recognition, rapport, respect, and advocacy—but most contacts stop short of genuine advocacy when stakes are real
When professional network promises go unfulfilled during a job transition, the most likely explanation is the other person's constraints, not a verdict on your value
The most useful thing a network provides is possibilities, not guarantees; expecting advocacy from a large network of contacts leads to repeated disappointment
quotes: You know the moment because it usually arrives after someone has said all the right things.
A former leader tells you they would love to work with you again.
A colleague encourages you to apply for an opening and offers to put in a good word.
Someone who praised your work for years says they would be happy to make an introduction whenever you need one.
Then an opportunity comes along, you reach out, and the silence on the other end tells you what the original conversation didn’t.
The relationship may have been real, but the offer was less solid than it sounded.
They answer, make the introduction, speak your name in the right room, and give someone a reason to take your call.

Other times, the thread goes quiet and you’re left trying to determine whether you misread the relationship, asked for too much, or somehow became less impressive between the enthusiastic offer and the moment you took them up on it.
